utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Same advice, if you have problems with translation, let me know. I see no notable absences in the Defence except for Bourgon. Prosecution team it's Ms. Soljan who I don't see this morning. So you were still in possession of the floor, Madam Nikolic and Mr. McCloskey. We hadn't concluded on the issue of proposed Exhibit P2013. I suggest that -- you were in possession of the floor, actually, when I stopped you, saying that it's time to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a couple of clarifications. Along with that exhibit, we have a table of contents that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- the Defence got which I think it would be a good idea to attach. We also had the index which had the slight description and the match or similarity which I think would be a good index to put in at the end. So if we could put the table of contents in the front and the index in the back, I think it would be -- then we will get hard copies for everyone and CDs for everyone. That would make, I think, a good approach to that exhibit. And that's all I wanted to say about that particular subject. Just a little more housekeeping on other issues, but if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Would that allay your concerns, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We had a meeeting about his before this session and we agreed that the complete material will be adequately marked and submitted to the Defence at the appropriate time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, with respect to this group of exhibits, I would continue to uphold my objection on the 36 aerial images and do not want those pictures or at least images at least at this time to be admitted into evidence at least engaged on the processes that we have engaged in on those specific aerial images.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to argue this matter with you, of course, because we are not here to argue with the parties, but on the other hand, don't you think that admissibility is one thing and final assessment of the probative value of those documents is another, depending on how the issue that we have debated relating to these aerial images will be resolved later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do agree with Your Honour that it's a two-step process; however, I don't believe they've reached or met their standard for the authenticity of those records and quite candidly we were stopped from probing because of the objection raised by the Prosecutor. And the Court itself I think mentioned that the pictures may be -- or the pictures may be different and we were, in my view, respectfully prohibited from further probing what the differences are and how Mr. Ruez was able in one or more pictures able to remove dates, which makes us suspect that they may not be authentic. I don't know that, but we certainly want to inquire of that issue. I don't believe it's met the first test, but I agree if it had, we would have allowed you to weigh those images.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further -- any further remarks on proposed 2013, P2013? And we are going to hand down our decision here and now. The document itself will be admitted or is being admitted as P2013; however, and I won't mention the exact number because I am not in a position to confirm that it is exact, the number of aerial -- US aerial photos, the authenticity of which have been contested will be temporarily marked for identification purposes only. And in due course we will reach a definitive decision on the admission or not. All right. They will form an integral part of 2013 for all intents and purposes, obviously; in other words, they are not -- they are only being singled out for future deliberation by the Trial Chamber. And I -- I also wish to underscore what you said earlier on, Ms. Nikolic, that is once more an indication of the spirit of cooperation that exists between -- between the two parties and which it is our sincere hope will continue. It will be in the interest of everyone to go -- to proceed along these lines, I can assure you. In other cases where it went wrong, where the client became contaminated, it was bad for everyone. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The videos that I mentioned, the individual numbers for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I take it those were admitted as well. There was no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any problems in relation to the videos that Mr. McCloskey mentioned yesterday? Do you want me to repeat the numbers? I am -- the 65 ter numbers, I can repeat them. I see no such request. I hear no such request, so they are so admitted. Each one separately. Madam Registrar, and it's your task to give them an exhibit number, which you will then communicate to the parties and to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit number will be exactly the same as the ERN number -- sorry, with the 65 ter number with a P before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you finished, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a couple of more housekeeping matters. I have been speaking with Defence counsel about the rule that's in place that each counsel provide the opposing party with the cross-examination materials at the time direct begins. And I think we all agree or at least close to agreeing, counsel may want to discuss this more among themselves, but that it's not necessary as far as we're concerned to provide those materials at the beginning of direct, that we're all satisfied that if those materials are provided at the beginning of cross. And we haven't been getting so many materials at the beginning of direct anyway, but I think it will allow that material to be more limited in the end anyway because they will be more targeted, having been able to think about it after seeing direct some. So I'm not sure we have complete unanimity on that, but I think we are close to it, but of course that's your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would just remind everyone that I have them here that if they have any questions or concerns about the US imagery, that we can get that in writing, that will help get the US going on this issue so we can get that resolved. That -- if there are particular concerns, that may help the issue. So I've said that. I just wanted to make sure everyone was aware of that. And regarding the recent motion about Obrenovic materials, we will be responding to that in the next day or two, but there was an unfortunate miscommunication because I had been communicating with the group about this and we had agreed with some people that we were trying to put this off for logistical, for many reasons, for concerns of one of the Defence counsel. So it's much more looking like either November or probably January or February, and had that been asked that could have been made clear. But we're in a process of speaking to all the various parties involved, but I don't think that's an issue. And on that note, there was a practice that I've seen in other courtrooms that might be a good idea here, where before a party files a motion they are required to go to the opposite party to try to settle it, or at least provide he notice. Because in that case sometimes we can -- for example, this one would have -- half the motion would have been settled and that may reduce litigation and it may, I think, increase communication. So I -- that is mentioned in the motion and I have not mentioned it to counsel beforehand. So I just wanted to mention that as something to consider. Also, we have spoken to Defence counsel and for logistical reason it's been better for us to do Mr. Van Duijn before Mr. Franken and so far I don't hear any objections on that and we would be switching the order, if that's all right. And that's it for that housekeeping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Going through this list were briefly. Last matter you mentioned, I think it's something that you discuss. Similarly, question of disclosure, when the Defence teams are supposed to disclose to you the documents that are -- et cetera. Once you have reached us an agreement, do let us know. We would be prepared to live with what you agree on. Question of US aerial images, I suppose the situation will be much better addressed by everyone once everyone is aware of the exact parameters imposed -- or conditions imposed by the US government. In relation to Obrenovic, we'll await your response. As to your appeal to the Defence teams to adopt different system approaching you beforehand, I don't think we can impose this on the Defence. It's a question which -- which you may talk about amongst yourselves. And if there is an agreement amongst you, of course it will save us and you and everyone else much -- much time. But it's not something that we can impose as on any of the parties. Now, Defence exhibits. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to tender into evidence four documents from our provisional 65 ter list. These are the documents: 1D00006, 1D00009, 1D00010, and 1D00012. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to have it in writing, as was promised, in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I asked for the -- such submission to be submitted in writing and I remember that I heard some positive answers from the Defence. So I would expect in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Judge Kwon. So these four documents are so admitted and marked accordingly. All right. Anyone else from the Defence teams would like to tender? Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'd like to tender Exhibit 2D0003. Just so the record's clear because it's our first document, if we have the correct document, if the Court doesn't mind if I just give you the date of the document. It's a two-page documented dated the 19th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it is so admitted 2D0003. Any further -- Madam Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, I would like to tender 5D19, 5D20, and 5D27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could remind me what is 5D20.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D20 is this document that was transmitted by the Bosnian authorities to Mr. Ruez containing a document in names ending with "CH."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which was used at the last -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Particularly, the last page of it. Yes. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm surprised -- no objection in relation to 19?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am of the view of the admissibility and weight rule, and I think you will be able to give that the appropriate weight that it's necessary. I -- these newspaper articles I don't find very enlightening, but I'm not objecting at this point to the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, Madam Faveau. These three documents are tendered, being so admitted, marked accordingly. All right. You will know exactly the exhibit number in due course. Mr. Krgovic, I suppose nothing. Mr. Haynes. Do you wish to tender any documents, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I didn't use any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. Any other preliminaries? Preliminary matters? None? Yeah, Madam Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yesterday I raised the issue of DutchBat documents. Yesterday afternoon we received a document from the Prosecutor. I can't say anything as to whether the Prosecutor had the documents or not. We heard a witness last week and yesterday and he said very clearly last week that they had obtained the documents with some difficulty, but they had got it from the Dutch authorities. If the Prosecutor tells me that they don't have the document, I will accept the statement, but I'd like to know exactly whether the Office of the Prosecutor had the document or not or has the document or not. That's the first problem. Second problem, this is already the second witness in a row for whom we don't have all the statements translated in the language of the accused. Last Friday we received two statements from a witness, and only one of them had been translated into Serbo-Croat. The other had not been. Rule 66 is very clear. All prior statements by a witness have to be translated in the language of the accused. I'm confident that the Defence can continue to enable the smooth unfolding of this trial, but rules have to be complied with, including Rule 66 and they have to -- the accused have to have all the statements in the language they understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. McCloskey, have you identified already which prior statement has not been translated into B/C/S that -- I'm phrasing the question this way because I don't know if we are talking of a protected witness or not because a witness hasn't been mentioned. So I prefer to phrase it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One second, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, even two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, in the meantime I think you can prepare the witness. We've practically finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I am aware of -- there was one questionnaire that we became aware of recently and we -- that should be translated soon. There's also a Rule 70 document which the -- under -- under an agreement with the Dutch, the Dutch government have allowed the witnesses to either stand on Rule 70 or not. And in this particular case, at this particular time when we saw this witness, he released this internal document, the constrictions of Rule 70. This just happened in his proofing session. So it went out for translation. So that's the explanation for that. And the other one is a questionnaire that went out to everyone -- well, a very long time ago. And somehow that slipped through the cracks of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, in relation to the general comment made by Madam Faveau regarding the DutchBat documents as such, would that be covered by what you have already stated or is there anything else you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We -- I'm not sure exactly what she's referring to when she says "the documents" or "those documents." As you know, UNPROFOR, UNMOs, DutchBat, Sector North, I mean there are so many military documents that there have literally been thousands provided to the Defence. We have done a -- a very -- a sustained effort last night for four hours with our best people to broaden that search to the parameters that we got with Ms. Faveau and we were able to with a very general use of the term DutchBat come up with a couple of interesting documents. So at this point I'm fairly confident that we've provided all that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the universe out there outside the Tribunal, there may be more internal documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If there are problems along the way, if you encounter problems along the way, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could have one minute, if we're through, just to change over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to reply to what has just been stated by the Prosecutor, but I'd like to do it in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We can do it later. In the meantime we can start your turn for cross-examination, which is still a long way away in any case. Mr. Boering, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've kept you waiting for 30 minutes, but you've had an occasion these last five minutes to see for yourself that we were busy engaged with procedural matters that infallibly arise every day, several times a day. I welcome you on behalf of the Tribunal and I thank you for making yourself available to give testimony in this trial. Before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand to you the text of the solemn declaration. It's an equivalent to an oath in several jurisdictions, and once read out that will be your solemn undertaking with us. Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hereby affirm that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. May I ask you what your present rank in the Dutch armed forces is and how you would like the Trial Chamber to address you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My current rank is colonel within the air force, and I wish to be addressed as Colonel Boering, that covers my rank and my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Colonel, and that's how you will be addressed. Very briefly, Mr. Nicholls is going first. He will, I think, spend about two days at least examining you in chief. He will then be followed by the various Defence teams. Now, I've just touched upon something that we have been concerned about. It's in your interest rather than anything that is problematic for us, but we would like you when you have time, the various Defence teams, to sit together again -- the Prosecution has no place in this discussion -- and see whether you want to or wish to retain the current procedure that you have adopted. In other words, that when it's the time for cross-examination, you start the Defence for Popovic first, and then Defence for Beara second, and then Nikolic third, and so on and so forth. Feel free if you wish to change this pattern, either on a permanent -- more or less permanent basis or an a case-by-case basis. To do so, I mean, it may be very cumbersome for Mr. Zivanovic, for example, to go first each time, having to go first each time. Similarly or conversely you may wish to retain the present system. But we enjoy you to have a frank discussion among yourselves and come back to us and tell us what your preference is and we will accommodate you, of course. So, Colonel, Mr. Nicholls is going first. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Two very small points. As you can see, Colonel Boering is speaking in Dutch, in his first language, so that may take a little more time for translation. Second is, I apologise, our estimate of the timing was off. That is because it did not take into account the videos which I plan to view with Colonel Boering. The last time he testified, those had already been played. I intend to play them with him, so I estimate that I will be about two hours longer than the estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Your full name is Pieter Boering?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you're of Dutch nationality?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're married with two children?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And currently, as you stated, you're a colonel in the Dutch army. Could you very briefly describe what your duties are, what type of work you're engaged in now.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work in Munster, that's the NATO headquarters in Germany, and I work there as an adjunct for the operations at this time. For example, we're busy deploying a NATO response force or other deployments such as Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to briefly go through your military career. You joined the Dutch army in 1978. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From 1982 to 1989 you served in Germany as an artillery officer?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From 1989 to 1993, you had various postings, including here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From 1993 to 2002 you had other postings including here in the Netherlands, also of course in Srebrenica and later in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Correct, but from 1993 until 2002 I worked in Germany, especially in Seedorf and from there he was seconded to various other sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. And you were promoted to colonel in 2004. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I should have asked earlier, you were born on the 6th of May, 1959. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. I want to go now to when you arrived in Srebrenica. Do you remember the date that you arrived in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was 3 January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was that your first lengthy foreign mission?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was my first foreign mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was there any kind of introductory meeting with the VRS soon after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Once we had been in the enclave for a week, we met with the leadership of the Drina Corps and other units. They were introduced to us, and they included the corps commander, who was General Zivanovic; and of the different brigades surrounding the enclaves, there were representatives as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was the general purpose of that meeting? What was discussed?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The primary purpose of the meeting was to -- was to introduce especially General Zivanovic and the contacts of the different brigades surrounding the enclaves and -- so that if we wanted to reach those people we could reach them as contacts. For example, the Bratunac Brigade, that would have been Major Nikolic. And in the Skelani Brigade, that was Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's -- you've just answered my next question, so that's good. Did General Zivanovic say anything about Srebrenica enclave and what he thought should happen to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: During the meeting, he briefly mentioned that he had owned a home in the enclave and that the task of DutchBat was to demilitarise the enclave, and that this in his view was our main task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, tell me what the DutchBat mandate was when you were there in 1995, briefly, what you recall it was.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Our mandate was first of all to secure the enclave; second, it was to demilitarise the enclave itself; third, to provide humanitarian assistance, especially within the enclave, but if possible also, for example, in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we'll talk about that mandate a little bit later. Could you tell me about how the DutchBat forces were organised in Srebrenica and how many companies there were, where the headquarters were.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The headquarters were in Potocari, and the staff and medical care was provided there as well, as well as one company that was guarding the northern section around the enclave. And in Srebrenica there was a bravo company that addressed the securing of the southern enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the name of the company in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: There was a charlie company and a staff company and the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness map 6, please, and that's IC00002.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that should appear on the screen in front of you, Colonel. If it doesn't, we have hard copies. I don't have it yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Nicholls, can I know the rank when he arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was your rank in January 1995, when you arrived in Srebrenica, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, while we're waiting for the map --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, maybe I should move to a hard copy, Your Honour, and just put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you wish, if that is faster. Why hasn't it shown up on the -- on e-court? Okay. Let's proceed. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour. I am told it is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, it is definitely in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. It's now up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, if you take a quick look at this map, which I think I showed you when we met last week. Is this map accurate in depicting the enclave and where the UN bases were?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that's a clear picture, but I'd like to shift it a bit further to the north because I don't see the bottom of the enclave -- no, no, other direction. That's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, these letters and points surrounding the enclave, N, O, P at the top, D, K, S at the bottom, what do those signify?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Those were the surveillance posts and they were generally permanently occupied by a bat, eight DutchBat crew members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And are those sometimes referred to as OPs, observation posts?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, those are the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever visit these OPs?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I visited most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were these observation posts -- we'll talk about this more later, but briefly, were they ever attacked by any armed forces?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, they were attacked by Serbian troops, especially at the end of our stay in the enclave, so in early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did observation post E at the bottom, echo, did that ever move its location?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At the end of the enclave in the early July, that post was indeed attacked and we retreated toward the city of Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were any new OPs created after observation post echo fell?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, they were created and in fact you could say that the road you see running from U to Srebrenica, along that road, various positions were taken there, later known as blocking positions, but also served as observations posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what were the main functions of these observation posts within the Dutch mandate?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Primarily to -- primarily reporting. Both people entering the enclave from outside and those leaving from within to outside, whether they were Serbian or Muslims, to secure the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in total, how many DutchBat soldiers were there approximately from January to July 1995 serving in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: About 400 or 450.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did that number stay the same from January to July or did it go up or down, change at all?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It decreased considerably, perhaps down to 300 or fewer, especially because more people were able to go on leave or for other reasons and were not allowed to return to the enclave because the Serbians didn't let them back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able ever to leave the enclave and return during your six months there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I went on leave once. I believe that was around the end of February. I had a week of leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about your duties with the VRS and with the ABiH. What was your position, your title, as a major in DutchBat in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The position I held was on -- was maintaining contact on behalf of the battalion commander, with both the civilian and the military leadership, both within the enclave and with the VRS side. So in that capacity, I was in touch with both the ABiH and the VRS military as well as with the mayor and the civil -- the local authorities. I also had contacts within the enclave with NGO organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me break that down a bit. Who were your contacts, your main contacts, with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: In the VRS, primarily the Bratunac Brigade, that would have been Major Nikolic. And a bit less frequently, but if problems arose, I'd contact the south, such as OP Echo, that would have been Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, just to avoid any possible confusion. I don't have it in my mind, but some might. When he says -- when he refers to Major Nikolic, he is not referring to the Nikolic that stands accused in this case; he is referring to Dragan Nikolic I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He is referring to Momir Nikolic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I've discussed that with counsel. I was going to try to establish that without leading too much. I believe the witness will identify Momir Nikolic later in a video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To clear it up. But you are absolutely right. We are talking about Momir Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, it was Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, where -- I'm sorry. I've -- Colonel Vukovic, who you would meet at the south by -- at the south end of the enclave, which brigade was he attached to, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was the Skelani Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Where -- first of all, how often -- you might have answered this, but how often did you meet with Momir Nikolic in general?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I would say once every two weeks, and if incidents occurred then we would try to initiate more direct contact and we would do that through a UN interpreter who was at -- stationed in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where -- when you met with Momir Nikolic, where would you meet him, typically?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Most meetings took place just beyond Observation Post Papa in the direction of Bratunac. There was a VRS observation post there, and sometimes we would continue on towards Bratunac to Hotel Fontana to talk in more detail. But most of the meetings took place right near OP Papa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was there a bridge there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes -- well, it's -- it's called "yellow bridge," but you couldn't really call it a bridge. It was just the designation. It was a through road between the observation posts and these Serbian posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what types of issues -- not talking about specific incidents, which we'll talk about a little bit later, but what types of issues did you talk about with Momir Nikolic when you met him?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At DutchBat we had some difficulties with convoys, both ingoing and outgoing. This was reported officially from Zagreb, but at a lower level. We were also told: We want that convoy, can you notify your leadership of that? Sometimes there were some messages from the enclave in the event about arranging meetings, and at a certain point when our supplies deteriorated a bit then the contacts about supplies were through them or an intermediary of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we'll talk about that in a bit more detail soon. Did Momir Nikolic ever introduce you to any superior officers?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Occasionally when I attended a meeting at Fontana or at the observation posts at yellow bridge, it did -- there were some appointments arranged at the instigation of Major Nikolic. And a higher-ranking member of the Serbian armed forces would be present, that's correct. And in those cases, he was the liaison to introduce somebody, and that other person would continue the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of the more-senior officers that Momir Nikolic introduced you to for meetings?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, I remember one name in any case, that was Colonel Beara. That was between March and April, and then again between May and June. Once there was a meeting at yellow bridge and the other time at Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The first meeting, can you briefly describe what occurred at that meeting and where it was, which -- whether that was at the Fontana or at the yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The first meeting, if I remember correctly, was between late March and early April. I don't remember whether it was at the request of Major Nikolic, but we were heading that way because the situation had become very tense. And then we shifted from our own observation post to the yellow bridge. There was a type of attack or ambush. We were -- there was ambush by the VRS, and ultimately we were taken to the yellow bridge. And there we found Major Nikolic and Colonel Beara, and I was introduced to them. What I remember is that at that point there was tremendous interest in these -- in whether a Muslim leader was in the city and what his position was. Naser Oric -- especially Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who was asking you about Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you -- what did Colonel Beara want to know, very briefly, about Naser Oric? What was he -- what was his purpose of meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Whether he was present, what his role was, and whether he might meet him, whether inside or outside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, whether Naser Oric would meet Colonel Beara; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you could describe the second meeting briefly with Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The second meeting in Bratunac at Hotel Fontana was -- if I remember correctly -- was at Major Nikolic's request. The meeting lasted at least half an hour, perhaps an hour, and also concerned the stay and information about the leadership of Naser Oric, how it was organised. And once again they were clearly looking for information about how -- especially the ABiH was organised in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And briefly, how did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls. If you could address the approximate date of this second meeting, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could tell us again, Colonel, the date of the second meeting. I think you said earlier between May and June, but if you can tell us when the second meeting was.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was in late May or early June. Exact date would be somewhere between the end of May and the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And briefly, how did Momir Nikolic behave when he was in the presence of you and Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the objection, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, the objection of a lack of foundation. This witness has not testified as to how Major Nikolic normally acted around other soldiers; and now the Prosecution wants to ask a question which has no foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can easily lay a foundation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear your response to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can lay the foundation. I was going to try to bring it up through the witness in reverse, but if Mr. Meek prefers, I can ask some more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think there's anything wrong with the way I phrased the question, but it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it may simplify matters if you do, but on the other hand, if you want to proceed with the same question you put before, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before you met with Major Nikolic -- with Momir Nikolic and Colonel Beara the first time, how many times had you personally met with Momir Nikolic on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think I met him about once every two weeks, so we're talking about March -- well, through March. I saw him at least six or seven times, and later in March there was a brief period of tension but we did ordinarily meet about once every two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you met with him as well between the first and second meetings when Colonel Beara was present, you met with Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How did Momir Nikolic first of all normally behave, how would you describe his sort of personality or demeanour around you when you met with him?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He was terse, business-like, had little time, and was to the point. From the Serbian side, he was in charge of everything at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was he friendly to you? Was he -- how did he behave to you on a personal level?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Very business-like. Straightforward. But friendly, no, I didn't notice any friendliness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you able to observe Momir Nikolic ever when he was around General Zivanovic, did you meet them together before you met with Momir Nikolic and Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him several times, once with Zivanovic, twice with Colonel Beara, and at the time he was clearly in the background and was the person to establish contacts and was not allowed to intervene in the discussion. He was more there in a secure -- in a security capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "at that time," which times are you talking about there where Momir Nikolic was in the background?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, for example, the meetings with Zivanovic or the meetings where he was with Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you notice - I'll ask it now - any change in the behaviour of Momir Nikolic at the meetings with Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. That's been asked and answered and it's repetitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You objected when the question was put and he hasn't -- we've gone in a round-about fashion to get there so that there will not be any objection at all. Now that we've come there, you say that he's answered that question. He's never answered that question. Yeah, go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can answer the question, sir. Did you notice any change in the behaviour of Momir Nikolic with Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He was more withdrawn and did not intervene in the conversation and it was clear his role was that of a liaison and not contributing active input at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, moving on to your contacts with the Muslim military, the ABiH, who did you meet on that side of the equation?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Naser Oric, at first the leader of the ABiH; Chief of Staff Ramiz Becirovic; and the third, Ekrem, who was ordinarily responsible for security, but in the absence of the other two, was sometimes in charge as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Anybody else that you recall from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, especially in the western part of the enclave under the aegis of Zulfo and there was a more independent area with its own leader. I met him once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we'll talk about that as well in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't mentioned any time-frame here, which is important I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you -- you were there from January to early -- to July 12th, 1995. Could you describe when you met with these different ABiH leaders, Naser Oric, Ramiz Becirovic, Ekrem, and Zulfo, if you can describe when you met with them during that time period.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: We generally met with the ABiH leaders about once a week. I think it was on Tuesday or Wednesday, I don't remember exactly, but it was a regular day if it was convenient to speak with them. And that was especially in the beginning, I had a few meetings with Naser Oric and Ramiz quickly took over from him in that respect. Zulfo -- it wasn't possible to meet with Zulfo personally. He was more of a loner and avoided dealing with us. I have a question. On my left screen I see a sketch of the enclave and at first I saw a text in English. Perhaps that text in English could be restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just approximately, when was it that you stopped meeting with Naser Oric and began to meet more with Ramiz Becirovic, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think it was in early or mid-February. It was clear that we needed to contact Ramiz and Naser Oric hardly ever showed up at the meetings -- or he showed up once or twice but unexpectedly. Ramiz was more responsible for the interactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And generally, briefly, what type of issues would be discussed at these meetings with the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The meetings between the military and the ABiH concerned how to act in the event of incidents such as disarmament. If we saw people who were armed, we were expected to intervene. And in the event of smuggling or when people broke out from the enclave, we would indicate: According to our information this happened. Can you confirm this? That was generally focussed on observations and verification. In Srebrenica an arms depot had been taken hold of, and that required maintenance. And the question was: When should the maintenance be performed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple of questions now about the VRS and then about the ABiH. Based on your -- since 1978 and you're in the Dutch army and as an artillery officer and your time in the enclave as the liaison officer meeting with Zivanovic, Momir Nikolic, Colonel Vukovic, and others, what's your assessment of the professionalism or organisation on the level of the VRS, as you could see it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Within the ABiH? Within the VRS the level of professionalism was clear -- it was clearly a hierarchical structure of a corps commander and various brigades and liaisons. It was very clearly defined, and if you had appointments and arrangements they were generally observed. As for arms as far as I could see, there were tanks, there was artillery, there were enough motorised vehicles. So logistically, there was sufficient military material. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you the same question now about your assessment of the ABiH armed forces that you observed and came into contact with in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The organisation was primarily in touch with the main leadership. It was divided into specific regions in the enclave, and I wasn't in touch with those people; the company was in charge of that. And if you consider the leadership style that was centrally present from the enclave, the western part was reasonably independent. There was almost no leadership necessary there. If you consider the lighter weapons such as fire-arms and some light mortars and anti-tank armaments, but there were no heavy tanks or sufficient logistical supplies. The only tanks present were at the munitions depot at Srebrenica in the beginning, and they weren't used for exercises or other matters; they were simply in storage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while we're here, what types of weapons did DutchBat have, your companies?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: We had -- we had certain type of vehicles with anti-tank arms, no heavy tanks or artillery, no heavy mortars, they were caterpillar vehicles, so limited armament and fire-arms. And the idea was that if something serious occurred, we were to report that and request air support, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just going back to the ABiH for a second, you talked about the clear hierarchical structure of the corps commander and brigades and liaisons in the VRS. How clear was the hierarchical structure and division in the ABiH, as you could see it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I didn't notice any clear role, but the leadership from Naser Oric and Ramiz. But there was a section in the west that -- Zulfo was responsible for that. That was relatively independent, and I don't think that Naser Oric or Ramiz were directing that. I think that nearly a thousand men within the enclave were -- were a group of soldiers who trained and exercised, but the real training and exercise -- I didn't see that. We assumed that nearly a thousand men could indeed act in the -- in such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, could he be a little bit more precise about this particular Zulfo. Becirovic, he mentioned him as Ramiz Becirovic. Oric, he said Naser Oric. With Zulfo we've got just Zulfo, and Zulfo, to my knowledge, is quite a common name in the area. If he could be more specific. Probably it's not a problem for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that -- we can do that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet this person Zulfo, who was, as you say, in charge of this more independent area to the west?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, I didn't exactly speak with him. I did meet him. That was I guess around February when there was a hostage taking near -- I believe it was Charlie Observation Post, it could be Bravo, but I believe it was Charlie and the leadership requested that I go there to try to get the Dutch -- that the DutchBat military who had been taken hostage be released, and I went there and saw Zulfo, but I didn't really speak with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So then just to be clear, these were DutchBat personnel who had been taken hostage by troops under Zulfo's command. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know Zulfo's last name? Do you remember it if you ever --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. We spoke about Zulfo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened when you went there to negotiate the release of these DutchBat soldiers who were being held on the western side of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I was taken hostage as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how many DutchBat soldiers were hostage at that time, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, about ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How long did this hostage taking last in total? How long were these men held hostage?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think it was about three day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did that situation end? How were you released?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: There was some discussions, not by me but I believe Colonel Karremans spoke to those in charge; for example, Naser Oric and Ramiz, so that they were ultimately able to mediate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And other than that Zulfo was in charge, so to speak, of this area on the western part of the enclave, do you remember anything else about him as a commander that you could tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Not from direct observation. Only the area for which he was responsible, which was known as the Bandera Triangle, he did not want any involvement by DutchBat patrols. In his opinion -- that was a no-go area as far as we were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was DutchBat able to control in that no-go area or did DutchBat stay out of that no-go area generally?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons why we were taken hostage at the time because we tried to patrol it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to go back now talking about the different people and organisations you met with as liaison officer. You said that you met with the civilian authorities and that you met with the mayor of Srebrenica. Did the civilian authorities report to you on the situation for civilians in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: We had weekly meetings with the mayor of the enclave. These meetings primarily addressed humanitarian concerns and any issues that he thought were important, he would raise them and discuss them with us. So you -- the humanitarian situation was the primary subject of discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll talk about that and the situation in the enclave after the break, which will be in a few minutes. Which NGOs or humanitarian organisations did you meet with?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The delegation of Medecins Sans Frontieres was there, Doctors Without Borders; there was a local staff member of the UNHCR and sometimes a UNHCR convoy entered; there was a local staff member of the Red Cross; and occasionally a small organisation that would enter with messages or a few small projects and then leave again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did these humanitarian organisations also report to you on the situation in the enclave for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Can we go into private session for a while, please? One moment, Colonel, before you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, all right. I just want to make sure we are in open session and no longer in private session. The public would be pleased to know that the last 30 minutes was break time, during which we were deliberating on some decisions that are in the pipeline. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to ask you my last question again and in your answer keep in mind what -- what we talked about just before the break. I don't want you to give the names of people. I don't want you to give specifics. I would just like to know whether in your duties as a liaison officer you learned, received information about the conditions for people in the enclave from the humanitarian organisations you described or that you had contact with. It's pretty much a "yes" or a "no" question.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as part of your duties you've talked about how you visited all of the observation posts, but how did you travel around the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Generally in a Mercedes jeep, and later from mid-May when our fuel started running low I did foot patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll talk about the situation later. That Mercedes jeep, is that a -- could you describe it. Was that an armoured vehicle or a sort of civilian jeep?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It's not an armoured vehicle. You could say it's a military jeep, but a civilian model, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did DutchBat have APCs at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, we had a few caterpillar vehicles available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If necessary, could you patrol in those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, our fuel started running low fairly soon, so as far as I remember I never used an APC on my patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You described the observation posts, that they were used to secure the boundary of the enclave and that they were manned by, I think you said, eight DutchBat soldiers generally. Can you physically describe for the Trial Chamber an observation post. What physically kind of structure that is and what kind of weapons, if any, are kept in an observation post.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, it's a somewhat elevated post, reinforced by sandbags and wood. The post is constructed with a view toward a good view, and there's -- there's -- it's lit so that you're clearly visible for all parties. And as far as being armed, there is -- there are firearms and perhaps some anti-tank weapons and IPR. There is small arms as well as a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what's an IPR?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It's an APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And physically how large is an observation post? You've described how it's elevated and it's lighted so everybody can see it, but how large is a typical observation post?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Big. Well, six to eight men could live there, sleep, and have a good view, so it's a small residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long would a shift be at an observation post for these six to eight men?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Generally one week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe for me, please -- you've described the observation posts and how they were -- the general structure, command structure of the DutchBat at the time. Who was the commander? Who was the deputy commander, and where you fit in in the command structure.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The battalion commander was Colonel Karremans, deputy was Major Franken, and within the battalion structure of which Karremans was the battalion commander, there were several divisions. And one of the divisions to which I belonged was the liaison division that maintained contact with the aforementioned military and civilian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I've never -- I've never been in military, but would you then report if you had any information to report to Franken and to Karremans or who would you report to?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, we had daily meetings. Perhaps on the weekend we might miss a day. We would have meetings with Colonel Karremans at his office and the division heads would attend, and we would report on what had happened that day. And every week we would meet and plan a bit further into the future. We also issued reports concerning our own field. For example, the civilian situation was something that we reported about to Tuzla, which was a level higher up than us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just -- just to be clear, who did you -- which command was in Tuzla that was reported to?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That was the north-east sector. Bosnia was divided into various sectors, and we were part of the sector in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to ask you some questions about the living conditions, the situation in the enclave for the population. Let's say now from -- break it up a bit, January through April when you arrived. Based on your observations and your contacts, first of all, could you tell me about whether there was enough food for the people in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Food was scarce. It was -- the incoming convoy contents were divided at the warehouse. Everything was in short supply, so a black market emerged where smuggled goods were sold at very high prices. Everything was clearly in short supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you know or if you can give your best estimate, how many people were living in the enclave at this time, the first few months that you were there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Perhaps around 30.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about water supplies for the population?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: There was a very provisional water system that was often broken and often malfunctioned, not only for the population but also for DutchBat. The water supply was generally bad. Sometimes I saw people standing in long lines at wells trying to pump water, and they would then have to walk a long way to get the water they pumped home again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about medical care for the population?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, the medical care -- there was a hospital in Srebrenica. We visited it a few times. And there was medical personnel supported by MSF, Medecins Sans Frontieres, and there was a -- there were a few local doctors' stations. And DutchBat also manned or ran some of those medical stations, but medical care was generally limited. Emergencies could not really be treated within the enclave, and there were often convoys of people headed toward Tuzla by bus for additional treatment. There was a hospital with limited medical supplies, but the supply levels were often difficult to maintain. And the medical equipment was another problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the problem with the medical equipment?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Either it wasn't there or it was broken or it was difficult to repair, so the state of the medical equipment wasn't good. So the support from DutchBat consisted of -- any military personnel that any knowledge about that would try to help get the equipment functional again. Sometimes we assisted with operations or other supplies as requested by the hospital or MSF or local civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear. You talked about supplies in general, but were there enough supplies of medicines, drugs for the population?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. Medical supplies were insufficient to meet the needs of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about fuel for the population, for the needs of the population? You already talked a little bit about how DutchBat didn't have enough fuel, but for the people who lived there.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was available in very limited supply. A few cars were riding around the enclave. Occasionally there were some mechanical chain-saws and there were some batteries, but there was generally no fuel. So the power supply came from generators powered by water, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I was going to ask you about that as well, but what about electrical -- electricity and supplies of that for the population?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Virtually nonexistent. Small number of people had generators that they used for connections and a bit of light in the hospital to get the equipment going. They used aggregates as generators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't quite understand that they used aggregates as generators.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: They used generators, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And finally the sanitation situation for all these people who lived in the enclave, what was that like?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, there were hardly any water-pipes or power, so personal hygiene and waste processing were difficult. Opportunities were limited for that. That was generally bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've told us -- started to tell us about how some of these shortages affected DutchBat, but if you could just specifically for you and the other members of the DutchBat battalion, tell me briefly about your supplies of food, water, and the sanitation and conditions for you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If you identify the time-frame, for example, from early May, it's fair to say that our fuel supplies and food supplies became very limited. We had to switch to emergency rations, and we also limited our vehicle displacements and tried to do more and more through foot patrols. There were also limited opportunities for purifying water and personal hygiene was also limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And these shortages and problems that you've described after you arrived in the enclave, how did those -- how was the situation of those problems during May and June and into the first week of July for the population? Did it get any better? Did it get worse?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It deteriorated considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I want to talk to you now -- you started talking about aid convoys. I want to ask you about those. How often aid convoys were able to come into the enclave in the beginning, and if you can tell us how that progressed during the time you were there, whether these convoys were able to continue bringing relief or not.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I assume you mean the relief supplies that UNHCR brought in for the population?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: These convoys with respect to number of vehicles per convoy and total number of convoys decreased considerably, especially obtaining clearance to pass through the Serbian area was a major limiting factor in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe how that process was supposed to work, the clearance through the Serbian area, and who on the Serb side was to provide clearance for the convoys to come through?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: As far as UNHCR is concerned, I wasn't personally involved in requesting convoys. But as for DutchBat, that went through Pale and authorisation would be issued as to which convoys and how many vehicles were authorised to travel certain routes, so that was subject to central direction there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked about the situation deteriorating considerably towards the end of your time, the last few months that you were in the enclave, and you just talked about the difficulty with assistance to the population. What were the other -- if any, what were the reasons why the situation deteriorated so much for the population towards the end?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, you might also say that over the course of May, June, July the threat increased from the Serbian side to the enclave. There were more shootings. At the end of June, one of those observation posts in the south, the Swedish Shelter Project, where quite a few refugees were residing, that couldn't exist anymore. So that part of the population withdrew toward the city of Srebrenica. So there was an influx of refugees even though the city was already filled with people and refugees. So the situation deteriorated because people became more insecure and drew closer to each other within the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said there were more shootings under the threat increasing on the Serb side in May, June, and July. Can you describe that a little bit. What was the situation of the shootings before May and then after May? Can you describe the shooting and shelling into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, I can't speak from May, but as of June and July I can. This varied from our own observations and members of our battalion who had made observations. This meant that from Potocari, our own quarters, we could see houses facing our camp being shelled from Bratunac, where at the time no people were present, that is in the house that they lived in. So in our own observations we could see shelling, shelling of houses. We were also told that this took place further south, but this is something I didn't see myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The homes that you saw shelled, just to be clear in your answer, were people living in them or were they vacant at the time that you saw them being shelled?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Normally speaking, would be living there, they could be lived in. For instance, there was laundry drying outside, which is a typical sign of people living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was living there? Who was living in these houses?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Members of the Muslim population of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where did these people go when their homes were shelled?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: They would move in the direction of their own village, Potocari, or towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you're talking about June. Can you tell me how frequently you personally observed shelling of homes in June?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: In June -- well, maybe two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we'll talk more about what you observed in July. How many reports of shelling -- you said you heard about shelling in the south and other areas. How much shelling did you hear about in June?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but at least I have heard about this a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During -- speaking now of June. Were you aware of any casualties from this shelling?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Obviously information was provided by the leadership of the local population and from hospitals about casualties. I did not see those casualties myself, so we received reports about people being hurt and people being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did this shelling affect your - not you personally necessarily - but DutchBat's ability to patrol the area?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: As to myself, late June -- late May/early June when leaving the compound in Potocari we would face direct fire on vehicles, shooting just in front or behind the vehicle, as a result of which with more frequent occasions we tried to avoid movements, which is why at some point -- I chose at some point to remain for longer periods of time in Srebrenica. Therefore, for me personally, it certainly did have effects on my movements about the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During this shelling directed at your vehicle, how close would these shells be to you as you -- as you travelled down the -- your route?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: 50 metres, approximately, which militarily speaking means pretty close.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said before when you were talking about the shelling of the town that it came from Bratunac. How could you tell that the shelling was coming from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: From where our camp is, when looking at the terrain one would see some hills outside the enclave. From there, the firing took place, which we could conclude from the sound. Initially I would drive around outside the enclave, so I knew that positions were situated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which positions are those? VRS or ABiH positions that are doing the shelling?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: These would be VRS positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And these shells that were landing near your vehicles you were patrolling with, 50 metres away, was that shelling from VRS or ABiH? Who was sending you that message?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I assume that this originated from VRS. Initially there has been a report about -- from the UN interpreter Petar in Bratunac who indicated that it was dangerous to regularly come inbound as we were doing with vehicles. So this was a warning to beware.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned this Swedish Shelter Project. Can you tell us what that was and how many people were living there at the time that they had to leave because of shelling.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I have been at the Swedish Shelter Project two times myself. It was in the southern part of the enclave near Sierra, near the Sierra observation posts which were situated in between. The project had been initiated, funded by the Swedish government. It was a centre with a capacity of 4.000 inhabitants, refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did -- and then all of these people, if I understood you correctly, these 4.000 refugees came into the centre of Srebrenica after the project was shelled. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: In any case, they left the projects because they were so insecure. This is why they left. This was because of shellings. I have not observed this myself, but I was informed about this by the local population, that this was the reason why they had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about the problems for the population with food, sanitation, medicine, convoys not arriving as they should. When you met with Momir Nikolic, did you raise these issues with him?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Not only on behalf of the command or with -- we did not only submit demands that Pale but also on the level of battalion, often we underscored the importance of convoys and supplies. We transmitted letters to be transferred to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what response did you get?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The replies obviously were that the letters would be passed on to the higher command, but that we would not receive positive news after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were any of these problems that you raised, addressed and dealt with and made more satisfactory after you made requests to the VRS to get any results at all?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If you mean aid convoys, not as far as I've been able to observe. But I have had no observation as to the exact dealings of the procedures in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, did you talk to Momir Nikolic at all about the shelling near the DutchBat base in Potocari and near your vehicle at all? That's two questions. I'll ask you if you talked about either of those topics with him.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, we did discuss these matters. This would happen either directly or indirectly through the interpreter Petar, who was also a liaison that we communicated with over the walkie-talkie.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did Momir Nikolic respond when you told him about this shelling from the VRS which was coming near the base?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he did not really react to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked earlier about how you went to a meeting -- I believe it was the first meeting you said where you met Colonel Beara with Momir Nikolic and there was an ambush by the VRS. I just want to be clear. Who was ambushed?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Myself on my way towards the meeting. This men in between the observation post of our own troops and the yellow bridge, in the direction of the yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And maybe if we could have map 6 up again, please, and we can see where this ambush took place. That's 00002. Still maybe if we can blow it up a bit in the section of Observation Post P. And I'm sorry, I don't remember how he can point -- can't he, to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
