utterances.text: We can do it. If you want to direct him to Observation Post P, then the idea -- you have that pointer incorporated in the e-court system. And we'll show Observation Post P and then fire the questions that you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If somebody could just show the colonel where the pointer is and how he can use that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he can identify the pointer by just looking at -- if he is on e-court mode, he should be able to follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay, Mr. Nicholls. I mean, these are fully understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, first if you see --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've made a little line by Observation Post Papa. Could you make a line across the road from Papa to Bratunac at the approximate location of the yellow bridge. You can't be exact on this map, but just how close the yellow bridge was to Papa.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has made a line across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Approximately where did the ambush take place? You don't need to mark it. If you can just tell us where it was in relation to the yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the witness has made a dot in between the -- just south of the yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you describe this ambush. What do you mean by an ambush? What happened?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was dark. Normally speaking, the area would be lighted but this light was turned off. And from both sides of the road, all of a sudden some soldiers appeared who, let's say, overtook me and apprehended me, led me away. The road was covered with some land-mines, and they made me step over these land-mines on a piece of wood, and that's what I recall. And after this I was led away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who else was with you, if anybody, when this happened?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: One colleague was with me. He remained behind and could therefore report this, let me say, hold-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just one more question on this. When you say that these soldiers apprehended you, how did they physically apprehend you? How did they stop your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Simply, I was threatened with a gun, a gun was turned at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you report this incident to Momir Nikolic when you saw him next?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. You get there and of course you mention what happened to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was his reaction when you reported this ambush by VRS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think before we get to that, he needs to explain how from this ambush he ended up meeting with Momir Nikolic just to say. Because there is a blank there that needs to be filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That he escaped. Did they escort him there? Did Momir Nikolic come for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After you led away and you walked through this area, that had been mined, on the pieces of wood, what happened next? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, I was then escorted to Colonel Beara and Nikolic who were present there. And at that point it was discussed that the situation with respect to the VRS was extremely intense and they were extremely interested in what was happening in the enclave, especially as far as Naser Oric's stay was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He still needs to explain how they escorted him to Momir Nikolic. Did he inform them that he was supposed to meet with Momir Nikolic? Or were they were already -- were -- and they were expecting him -- him and the other person who was with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you explain that, Colonel, a little bit more. What did these soldiers do once they had, I think you said, abducted you. Did they immediately take you to the meeting or did you then explain to them who you were and where you were going?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Of course first you run into a language problem. You can't communicate with the people threatening you. And then without any communication you're threatened and they demand that you come along with them. And it wasn't clear to me where I would be taken at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did they take you? Did they put you in a vehicle or march you or --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I was taken away on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where were you taken? Just directly, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was a walk of about 50 or 100 metres in the direction of Bratunac near the yellow bridge and a Serbian post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened there at the yellow bridge?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Major Nikolic was there with Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did they have an interpreter with them?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, an interpreter was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What did you say to Major Nikolic after you'd been brought there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I expressed my indignation and asked what the problem was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't seem to recall, but was this meeting with Momir Nikolic asked for by your witness? In other words, was it planned already? And if it was planned, did he have any directions as to where it will be held, where he was supposed to go, whether he would need to stop at some particular place? I think we do require this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you explain that, Witness, how this meeting came about, whether you were invited to meet with Mr. Nikolic or whether you had communicated that you would like a meeting and were coming. How did the meeting come about and did Momir Nikolic know that you were coming to a meeting with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I believe since it was already dark at that time that it was an announced contact, whether it was from the DutchBat, through the interpreter to the leadership saying we went to speak to them, or through Nikolic, I don't remember how that worked. But the meeting place was a standard meeting place from OP Papa. Sometimes we drove there in a vehicle so that would be a 200 or 300-metre distance; other times we went there on foot. In this case I simply went there on foot through the no man's land to a well-known site where we often established contact and decided where we would conduct the meeting there or whether transport would be arranged in the direction of Bratunac for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what were you wearing and what was the other person who was with you wearing as they walked to this meeting? Were they -- were you in uniform or can you describe how you were dressed?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: We were wearing our military uniform and had our helmet and a bulletproof vest and a handgun.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, is that a blue helmet?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I understood your answer earlier, the meeting place you were walking to was a standard place where you would go to meet and you would go there sometimes on foot or sometimes driving, but that is where you would make contact with the VRS. Can I ask you again, do you remember with this meeting whether it was one you planned or just on your way there in order to try and arrange a meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I'm not entirely certain, but I'm assuming that it was arranged by the VRS, particularly because it was already dark and it's not our choice to proceed through a no man's land in the dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when you met with Momir Nikolic and Colonel Beara and you explained, as you said, that you weren't happy about this, what was Momir Nikolic's reaction?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: His reaction was limited, basically that this is part of it, and I was put through immediately to the person accompanying him who had some questions from me. That was his main concern. That was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, what do you mean basically that this was part of it? I'm not clear on what you mean by that, if it was a correct translation.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, it was part of the game. This was part of the enclave and guarding it and the tension between the military forces -- well, that's part of being in the military. Sometimes you're exposed to danger or surprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to talk now about a different topic. You talked earlier about the supplies for DutchBat were not getting through, therefore you didn't have enough fuel, not enough food, things like that. What I want to ask you now is: Did either the ABiH or the VRS take, steal, DutchBat equipment or property that you're aware of during the time that you were in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, thieves are everywhere, people who steal things from you both within the enclave. Military items would sometimes disappear and that would be the ABiH or another unknown party. Outside the enclave I at some point saw VRS soldiers wearing DutchBat gear, blue berets, T-shirts, and the like when I was en route from Potocari to Bratunac. I probably saw that by coincidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How often or how many times did you see outside the enclave what you took to be VRS soldiers wearing DutchBat -- parts of DutchBat uniforms?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Maybe once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever report that to Momir Nikolic, that you'd seen VRS soldiers wearing DutchBat property?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Of course I reported that, and there was no response.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What do you mean no response, that he wouldn't say anything or that -- could you describe that just a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, you'd indicate that you noticed something and you'd say: Something should happen. Fine. You saw that. I'm not going to do anything about it. I'll see what happens. My feeling was that nothing would be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to finish off this line, was anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask the Colonel whether he thinks that those might have been -- must have been stolen. Do you mean it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was -- somebody absconded with it, stole it. Somehow somebody must have got ahold of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, besides berets, what else, if anything, of DutchBat equipment did you see with VRS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Later on in July I saw some APCs that had probably been appropriated when the observation posts were taken. And I saw Serbian soldiers were already in there. That was near Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll talk about that a little bit later as well, as we get to that period. I want to talk to you now about some of the efforts DutchBat made in its mandate, as you've defined it for us. I'll start first asking you about demilitarisation of the enclave. First of all, you described at the beginning of your testimony how General Zivanovic at this introductory meeting said that the most important thing was that the enclave be demilitarised. Did he say anything else about the enclave, what would happen if it wasn't demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he mentioned that if this didn't happen it would have no more right to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What -- do you remember what he said, what words he used?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you remember that at the time you gave a statement to the ICTY in 1998 when you were asked about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I can't remember at this time. That was a while ago, but I did make a statement to the ICTY in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember talking about this first meeting with Zivanovic in that statement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember that he had formerly lived in the enclave and believed that it should be disarmed and that he wanted to return to the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would it help you remember to look at this statement that you made way back in 1998, much closer to the events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, if you think it is necessary to refresh the witness's memory. Go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to do without anybody jumping up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You made me jump up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can read to you, this is on page 3, for my friends, of his 1998 ICTY statement. ERN number 00583505. "General Zivanovic delivered a long speech during the reception, explaining that he had a house inside the enclave and that he would like to return there. He also said that the enclave had to be demilitarised by DutchBat, otherwise it would be razed to the ground." Now, does that help you to remember what he said at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. I endorse this. It was indeed said that way, but it's difficult to remember it exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand, and this statement was made quite some time ago. I don't expect you to remember everything perfectly; I don't think anybody else does. Now, then, talking about the efforts to demilitarise the ABiH in the enclave, in your view, was DutchBat able to accomplish this task?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: With the number of soldiers we had in the enclave, that was difficult to do. The right to conduct house searches based on suspicions, that was a fairly complicated procedure if I remember correctly. It was rather that if you encountered people while you're on patrol and those people were armed, then the idea was to confiscate the weapons of those people, but a focussed approach including house searches, that wasn't something that was happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When these arms -- you started talking before about an arms depot. When DutchBat patrols did see persons with arms inside the enclave, where would they -- and they were able to confiscate the weapons, where would they be taken and stored?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: They would ultimately end up in the Srebrenica weapon collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where was that collection point?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That was on or very close to the Bravo Company base in Srebrenica, so that was within the area guarded by the Bravo Company. So to gain access you had to have permission from DutchBat to get in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And say by the time the enclave fell, 11 July, how many -- how many weapons were being held in the arms depot and what types of weapons were held there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: There was some containers with fire-arms and some small arms and some larger anti-tank weapons and perhaps some rather obsolete tanks. I'm not sure whether they could really be deployed, and some munitions, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just one follow-up, fire-arms, small arms, if you can be a little more specific what types of weapons you're referring to, if you can be.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Machine-guns, rifles, handguns. They were often relatively outdated. Not ordinarily state-of-the-art military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During the time you were in the enclave, you already said that it wasn't possible for DutchBat to completely demilitarise the enclave. Are you aware of whether the ABiH was able to smuggle weapons into the enclave while DutchBat was there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Smuggling was clearly going on, otherwise the black market would not have existed in the enclave, and that weapons were being smuggled in as well seems obvious to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked earlier about the place you were held hostage on the western side, the Bandera Triangle as a no-go zone. It probably goes without saying, but I take it that you weren't able to demilitarise this area?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: My answer is yes. If it's virtually impossible to get in somewhere, then you can't do your job properly there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was the ABiH able to have any helicopter flights into and out of the enclave while you were there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. That happened on occasion and occasionally there were helicopter crashes where some people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was DutchBat able to control these helicopter flights by the ABiH? In other words, authorise or prevent them?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The idea was for this not to happen and for us to stop that, to prevent this from happening. And we tried to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just as you're aware, how many times did you learn that a helicopter had flown in or out, an ABiH helicopter?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: About five times. Often you -- you would learn about it through rumours among the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you know, typically are these flights during the day-time or night-time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Of course they were at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, as for weapons smuggled in, can I hear from where were those smuggled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, Colonel, you've talked about how there was smuggling going on. There was no question about that. There was a black market. You thought weapons would have been smuggled in as well. Do you have any information of where those weapons were smuggled in from, where they came from?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't have any data on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Talking a little bit now about the mandate to secure the enclave, you talked earlier about the observation posts, some of them being taken over by VRS troops. What I want to ask you know is if you know whether or not ABiH forces within the enclave were able to mount attacks outside the enclave during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That did happen, and we heard about that from Momir Nikolic; he would urgently request us to do something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to prevent such raids, we'll call them?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: We tried to stop it whenever we could, but it's fair to say that they were quite adept at circumventing the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "They" meaning the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you've also talked earlier and we'll talk a bit more about it soon whether there was shelling from the VRS into the enclave, shooting into the enclave from the VRS. Unfortunately, DutchBat was not able to stop that either. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: We didn't have the opportunity and lacked authorisation to patrol outside the enclave. So we had no knowledge of what the VRS did outside the enclave and certainly were not in a position to influence what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Reading through the transcript here, one would get the impression -- one would understand that the information about these attacks by ABiH forces outside the enclave but from inside, knowledge of this he obtained from Momir Nikolic. Did he or DutchBat or UNPROFOR, whatever, also have intelligence confirmation of that, independently of the reports or complaints of Momir Nikolic? Could they confirm them independently, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you answer the question from the Bench, Colonel. Based on your work in the enclave, your patrols, your intelligence, your contacts with the ABiH and other parties there, were you able to confirm the complaints from Momir Nikolic that these attacks had taken place?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't remember that, whether that was possible. Of course we would have liked confirmation in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you -- did DutchBat - not you personally - but did DutchBat make efforts to investigate these raids and what was taking place?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, you're getting into an area where I was not involved, but I assume that the battalion commands asked the same question to Tuzla and Zagreb and requested additional information asking: Can you tell us anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're a little bit earlier, but I'm going to move into a new chapter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you know how this Chamber operates. Whenever it's more convenient to you, we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same applies to you, Colonel. If at any time during your testimony you require a short or long break, please do let us know straight away and we will accommodate you immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we've been informed that Madam Faveau and Mr. Ostojic would like to address the Trial Chamber not in the presence of the witness. Mr. Ostojic, you go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Forgive me for raising this issue somewhat untimely. When we asked about the exhibits I failed to mention the one-page document that Mr. Ruez on the 15th of September actually drew with a red pen a route, and if you remember it was from the group of 272 exhibits, the first page, so it would be page 1. And Mr. Ruez wrote a route where the military column went and I think indicated two areas at least where they were battles or ambushes and I failed to introduce that as an exhibit and I did mention it to my learned colleague, so he is aware of it as well. Forgive me for wasting your time on this issue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there is a problem on your side, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it is so exhibited and it will be given a 2D exhibit thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Okay, because -- can you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have to start again, unfortunately. Okay, I think we are fine now. Could I kindly ask you to start all over again, Madam Faveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I would like to respond to the Prosecutor regarding a document that according to us must be somewhere in the Prosecutor's office. We are asking to get a daily report from DutchBat that were going to Srebrenica to the seat north-east which was in Tuzla, to the seat north-east of UNPROFOR, as well as the reports that were going from DutchBat to the to Srebrenica to the Defense Ministry of the Netherlands. Since the witness we had here the last few days was the chief investigator of the Prosecutor's office said -- and he said this yesterday on page 63, line 9. He said that the Prosecutor's office received all the reports of Dutch soldiers. We are not talking about witness statements; we are talking about daily reports that must exist somewhere because DutchBat is a military unit and as such they were sending daily reports to their superiors. We deem that these documents are absolutely of paramount importance for our case and that this case cannot be elucidated without these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Faveau. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What exactly Mr. Ruez meant is -- he knows that there's thousands of Dutch -- Dutch reports, UNMO reports, various reports related to this incident. He's familiar with the to and froing of trying to get documents from all these governments. But this asking for documents that must be in our possession doesn't -- doesn't help us and it's -- as you know, many times because there's so much stuff, we -- we're not exactly sure what's in our possession at times and I acknowledge that. However, we have done searches over several years under the names of all these various people, Franken and Van Duijn and the various witnesses. And we have recently done a very broad search regarding DutchBat itself and we came up with some 2.000 documents last night and we looked through those. It's my best opinion now that internal DutchBat reports we do not have. Now, of course there's going to be internal -- some internal DutchBat reports that are -- that are different from some of the UNPROFOR and other reports that we've seen. That -- if they exist, that has been known for years by any Defence and we had a request to assist them with the Dutch government. We could have got that. We still can, but as far as I know this material is not in-house and it's probably considered Rule 70 by the Dutch. Much of the material that we received was received under Rule 70 and we've been able to clear some of it. We're ready to assist the Defence if they can give us any more clear idea of what they're looking for, but I think I know what they're looking for and we don't have it. And if they want to get into the internal documents, let's get a request in, but this is the Nth hour, this is something that they could not have been years ago, years ago literally. And there are so many reports related to DutchBat, they were debriefed so many times and they testified so many times, the amount of information about what they've said about this is voluminous. Could it be helpful to have their internal reports? Yes. If this group of Defence attorneys wants that, we'll assist them in doing that and there should be enough time to do that and we will of course make an effort to bring people back if something comes up that's important. But right now my best view on having some very good people, including Ms. Faveau, who is very good at searching EDS, none of us have been able to find this material, aside from a few documents that we were able to find. And we have gone, as she knows, to Geneva, in the long ago past, and found some information. But it's an issue that we can help and we'll do our best to get stuff. But as far as I know from our best people looking, these things are not in our possession right now, and I don't -- the difficulty of getting materials, internal materials from governments, you know, is something I don't want to get into. I think we can probably get at this stuff if every -- if we do a concerted effort, we'll do an RFA and we can get at it, but it's a bit late in the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not asking to obtain the internal documents of the DutchBat, its internal documents of the Dutch authorities and government of Holland and documents that are within the Ministry of Defence, but there is a second batch of documents and those are documents that the DutchBat was to send to the north-eastern sector of Tuzla. These are the UNPROFOR documents, United Nations documents. Yesterday Mr. Ruez was very clear since I have asked him two very distinct questions regarding these documents belonging to the UNPROFOR. Mr. Ruez said that, yes, quite possibly or quite probably the Prosecutor's office has those documents and I think that Mr. Ruze is the person in -- who can definitely tell us if these documents are in the possession of the Prosecutor's office. However, I have no proof, I have no reason to doubt Mr. McCloskey's word, but in that case I think that the Defence can try, that is certain, but it would be much more efficient if the Prosecutor's office asked the Dutch government or the United Nations to obtain these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues before telling you or giving you a direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the position that we take is one which I am sure you would be anticipating, namely at -- as the situation is, we have to accept your word, Mr. McCloskey. We also understand that you're still not exactly fully happy with this situation. If you continue this discussion amongst yourselves and the Prosecution, upon your request, seeks or asks for further documentation from the Dutch government, of course we can look into that at a later stage when it happens. But we do understand the position of both of you, and it is also obvious that the Prosecution has taken very seriously the point raised by you yesterday and they have done a thorough search. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think it's a fair request. We'll work to get the wording of an RFA and get the Dutch on it as soon as we can. It's -- and we'll continue looking in that little pile of material that you know is over my shoulder and if we come up with anything we'll of course let them know immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But again I -- I regret we haven't -- I don't have my hands on this stuff, but if any -- these kinds of requests, the sooner we get them the better they are. But we'll get on it right now and get what there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, that's perfect. Thank you so much. Let's re-admit the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I recall the procedure, I would now like to save this image and give it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But he will initial it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct, we're coming to that exactly because it's still on the screen and I don't quite know whether we have finished with it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colonel, the image that should still be on the screen in front of you, we're going to save that and I'd like, if I could, for you just to put your initials in, say, the top left-hand corner. You can do it with that stylus.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Even better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you're tendering that map, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, and I suppose they all get tendered at the end, but if it gets a number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can get a temporary -- the number that will be assigned to it later on, at least temporarily for the purpose of the continuation of the cross-examination -- examination-in-chief and the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be temporarily IC7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic has pointed out to me that it should be dated, but I think it gets a date stamp automatically when this is saved or when this was created? I thought it got a date and time?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'm now going to ask you to tell us about the events that led up to the fall of Srebrenica and the week preceding the 11th of July, 1995. I'd like you as much as you can in your own words to describe what happened, what you observed, during this time. So let me begin around the 6th of July, where were you staying, at Bravo or at Charlie and what did you see happen that day? Let's start with the 6th.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 6 July I was still staying in Potocari. In fact, as far as I can remember, some observation posts had already been taken by the Serbians. The personnel from two observation posts had already been taken prisoner at the Swedish Shelter Project in the south of the enclave which was virtually deserted. On or around that date, a grenade badly hit our camp at Potocari, which was analysed by the EOD crew. Overall, things were very tense in the enclave. The city was fairly packed with refugees. The EOD is the Explosives Clearance Service. And riding from one site to another became more dangerous, so around 6 or 8 July I imagine that I stayed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you a couple of questions. If you remember, when did the observation post first start to fall or be taken by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that would have been at the end of June or early July. I don't exactly remember the date. I assume it was in early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you remember, roughly, can you tell me the order in which the OPs fell.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was especially in the south. I expect that it was Echo and then Sierra a bit further to the north, but I don't have the map in front of me depicting the different observation posts --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and bring it out a bit. It doesn't need to be the one that he marked, although it can be if you can zoom out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you see that all right? It's -- that's better. Thank you. Maybe a little bit -- bring it up a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine. I expect that was Fox-trot, Echo, and the rest of the sequence hasn't stayed in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be very clear, Fox-trot is the base marked F, Echo is the base marked E on the map?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you talked about the -- it says in the transcript "grenade" that hit the camp in Potocari. Can you describe what kind of explosive device that was. Is it a grenade that's thrown by a soldier, a shell, a mortar? Just tell me if that's correct what we have here or if it was something else?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it was a grenade from a piece of artillery or a larger mortar, based on the report of the -- of the hit as drafted by the EOD. Because there were quite a few projectiles flying back and forth around the compound. So I assume that it was artillery or a heavy mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Describe a bit more what you mean by "quite a few projectiles flying back and forth around the compound." What kind of projectiles? Where are they coming from?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a few projectiles, it's -- you -- I heard shots being fired from Bratunac, from the east, and then you could hear a projectile whistling across the compound. And then you would hear the impact and how many there were, a few, around that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how close were these impacts to the compound?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one was a few hundred metres away, and it's no longer clear in my mind where the others hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. How did this shelling affect DutchBat's ability to go out and patrol and see what was going on outside?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seriously limited what we could do. Generally, a bunker alarm would ring and the only patrols were those that were absolutely necessary. It became very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you become aware of other places being shelled within the enclave? Other objects?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at any rate from the report of a patrol and somebody told me personally that he had seen in the south of the enclave that villages were being -- were under fire and that the population was being driven into Srebrenica -- the city of Srebrenica itself. That was in late June or early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were these Muslim or Serb villages being shelled?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslim villages in the enclave itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then moving on, we've been talking about the 6th to the 8th. You described events on the 9th and into the 10th. What happened, what you experienced?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that point the city of Srebrenica became more and more crowded with refugees. The local population was very tense, and the military leaders of the enclave, that is, the Muslims, had a meeting around that time to plan how they would take it from there. And we met with them briefly. Colonel Karremans and I participated. Generally the situation was very tense and we lacked prospects.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was -- what was discussed at the meeting as terms of options how to deal with the VRS advance?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed how we might possibly put up a combined defence. It was a difficult discussion as to who would do what and whether it could be coordinated. And the second subject was the air support from -- that would be provided by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And before we get to that let me ask you a question I should have asked you a couple of moments ago. When these observation posts fell and were captured, were any DutchBat soldiers captured by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were taken prisoner. At one point the DutchBats that had been taken prisoner contacted us by radio and told us where they were. So we were in very limited contacts with the DutchBat people who had been taken prisoner. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many, approximately, DutchBat soldiers were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 10 or 15. I don't remember the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where were they being held? You said they told you where they were being held.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, while we were in radio contact, I didn't know where they were being held, but later on when they were being held in Bratunac I saw that it was in Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we'll get to that part as well. Did you -- do you remember a Dutch soldier named Rensen?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember him. Unfortunately, he was killed there by a hand-grenade that was most probably thrown by a Muslim fighter, and according to the Muslim leaders that fighter was not in his right mind and the Muslim leaders apologised afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was that killing by the Muslim of Private Rensen discussed at this same meeting you referred to a few moments ago where you met with the ABiH authorities?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that did come up in the discussion, but I believe that happened somewhat earlier at a different meeting. With Ekrem or Pejzovic [as interpreted] or Ramiz, I believe, we discussed it perhaps one or two days earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can the Colonel indicate to us the approximate time-frame when Officer Rensen was killed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, we're discussing this period. But as precisely as possible, do you remember the date when Private Rensen was killed by that hand-grenade?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date, but I assume it was in -- at the end of June or the beginning of July, probably the beginning of July but I can't say that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I have one moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could ask him whether at the time any of the observation posts had already fallen or not that would help him remember better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, you've His Honour's suggestion. Do you remember when this death was in relation to the fall of the OPs?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had lost Echo by then in any case. So the Muslim population was already tense at that, that the DutchBat was retreating a bit. That -- I can place that in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I may perhaps refresh his recollection from his first ICTY statement. He discusses this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from the first statement, 28 September 1995, on page 4 of the English, 00443270 is the ERN number. I'll read what you said in your statement, Colonel, and see if that helps you remember a little bit. The paragraph above starts: "One night on or about 8 July I heard heavy shelling ..." And you discuss the shelling and some other points. And the next paragraph you begin: "Private Rensen was killed around this time by a fragment of a hand-grenade that pierced his neck." Do you think that's accurate?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly as I remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a very classical example of leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's why I asked permission to read to him the portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we gave him --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I mean, I think the objection could have been before I started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, back to the meeting you went to with Karremans and the ABiH leaders. Can you tell us if air strikes or air supports were discussed and what conversations surrounded that issue.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conversation was with both the military leaders of the enclave, such as Ramiz, the mayor was also present, and the conversation was conducted by Colonel Karremans himself. And it was stated with some degree of certainty that air support was provided the next day. The support was provided to the population and the leaders; I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were there any conditions that had to be fulfilled before air support would be called in, anything in particular would have to happen?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what was known as the smoking gun principle. It certainly emerged during the days that preceded, they wanted -- the UN demanded evidence of attack. So we needed evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened as evidence provided?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was before the meeting with the leaders, perhaps the day before. I had a question earlier than that with Ramiz and I informed him of the need of a smoking gun. And -- well, let's say that they tried to comply with that. The Muslim military men said: This is what's wrong, and then a limited patrol advanced to see what was wrong. But when exactly did that happen, I assume it was before the meeting, one or two days before that meeting happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you know, where did that patrol go and what happened to that Muslim patrol?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: A patrol left Srebrenica toward the Swedish Shelter Project in the south, and they came under fire. I didn't see that myself, but there was a report. Some people were injured and perhaps killed among the Muslims. And they subsequently returned and -- well, let's say that wasn't sufficient evidence yet for air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell me now -- just continue with this topic. What happened, whether air support was eventually called for.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the end there has been a very limited amount of air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe that. What -- how many planes, what happened, and when it occurred, this limited air support.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I haven't witnessed this myself, so this is only from indirect observations. But as far as I understood, there have been one or two aircrafts that -- that could supply support for DutchBat vehicle that was under attack. So we are talking about a very limited amount of air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And let me go back one minute, sorry. When you talked earlier about meetings where Ramiz, is that Ramiz Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was it Commander Karremans who requested that air support and the limited air support arrived?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I assume, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is also a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a leading question, but I would suggest that you pop up in a timely fashion because, for example, he is -- it was a very short question, it has already been answered. And in any case, I mean not much harm -- not much harm done, I mean, because it could have easily been formulated in a different manner without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will try to avoid, Your Honour. I thought that was one I could use to move things a bit quicker, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the VRS reaction to these air strikes on their positions?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, at that point contact was made by the soldiers imprisoned in Bratunac saying that air support endangered those who had been taken prisoners and therefore it should stop. I have been informed of a report of this approximate content, so this was a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was the threat to the soldiers imprisoned in Bratunac? What would happen if the air strikes continued?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, this was not clear to me, but my impression was that things would be not good for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be very clear, which soldiers being held in Bratunac are we talking about? From which armed force?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were DutchBat troops, soldiers that had been taken prisoners from the observation posts taken over by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you know, is -- you've called it a threat. How was that conveyed to DutchBat in Srebrenica, by [Previous translation continues] ... that information?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, this was a radio transmission from Bratunac via our own radio receiver. A vehicle that had been captured, a DutchBat vehicle, had its radio used in order to transmit the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did air strikes continue after this message was received or what happened?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that I have seen no further air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the term "blocking positions" as a military term?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One might say that the observation posts that had been taken over or from which we had withdrawn and from which troops retreated to Srebrenica later on took positions that would allow to observe and provide protection. Such positions may be called blocking positions, as was the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And if you can just -- I guess you can't point on the map. I don't know that we need to mark this, but can you just tell us on the map that's before you, we see Srebrenica Bravo Company and below OP Echo and OP Sierra or S, where were those blocking positions located?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From, for instance, you have heard the road towards Kolov. This is a very windy road along which several positions were taken. Later on you see this with the entry into the city itself. A little bit further north from Kolov.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'll ask you to just mark it again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, or if you have a better map you can make use of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you can mark the approximate locations where the blocking positions were set up after the OPs fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have now indicated this with global markings along this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For the record, that's the four marks in between Echo --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And later on further north even towards the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if you could kindly put your initials next to any of those markings, either on the left- or on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay, it's okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, maybe we can do this just before we have to stop. Can you tell me about where the population from Srebrenica went. You talked about how people were crowded into Srebrenica and the shelling, the blocking positions, the OPs falling. Can you tell me where the people went next from Srebrenica. I'm talking about now the 9th, 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population mainly moved toward the city of Srebrenica itself. Close to the city the area was full with people. Houses were packed with people. A crowd of people had regrouped within and around the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were in Srebrenica at this time. How did those people appear to you, their physical state, their mental state, how they felt?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I have walked through the city at several occasions, also because I had to move towards the Bravo Company that -- from the Bravo Company to the place where the Muslim leadership was situated. Walking through the city, I could see people looking very apathetically, hungrily, very nervously. People were at a loss, asking you what was to happen to them, asking me what could we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where did you go on the 10th of July from Srebrenica, where did you go next, you personally?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I subsequently moved to the UN base near Potocari with the DutchBat soldiers that were stationed in Srebrenica. This happened at the moment when the situation had become hopeless, when the population started moving towards Potocari by its own initiative, when the wounded were transported from the hospital towards our camp in Potocari. If I remember correctly, the defences of the Bravo Company were no longer held and were run over by the Muslim population. So at that point the soldiers accompanied the flow of refugees towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This may be the last question today. Were you aware on that day about civilian casualties from the shelling?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, one mortar grenade came down close to the Bravo Company, which wounded a little boy who was brought to the Bravo Company to a shelter where I was myself, where he was given first aid. So there were people hurt in the close vicinity of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think this would be a good time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Colonel, I thank you so much. You still have a few days more with us. Not tomorrow, however, because tomorrow we have plenary, as we have previously announced. So we will not be sitting. Mr. Nicholls will presumably continue and finish with his examination-in-chief by the end of the week. So he will take the whole of Thursday, as I take it, and the whole of Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I won't take all of Friday for sure. I hope to finish Thursday. I may go into Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's putting on notice whoever will go first from the Defence teams with cross-examination. Please be ready. All right. Once more, thank you so much, Colonel. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls and the rest. We'll re-convene on Thursday morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
